extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, newspaper editors, media historians, and press professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes historical and professional standards, ethical canons, legal precedents, and operational practices governing newspaper journalism, advertising, circulation auditing, and press–government relations. Useful for understanding evaluative criteria for newspapers and journalistic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: A.S.N.E. Canons of Journalism — Responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement of the primary function and obligations of newspapers: 'The primary function of newspapers is to communicate to the human race what its members do, feel, and think. Journalism, therefore, demands of its practitioners the widest range of intelligence, of knowledge, and of experience, as well as natural and trained powers of observation and reasoning. To its opportunities as a chronicler are indissolubly linked its obligations as teacher and interpreter.' Canon I — Responsibility: 'The right of a newspaper to attract and hold readers is restricted by nothing but considerations of public welfare. ... A journalist who uses his power for any selfish or otherwise unworthy purpose is faithless to a high trust.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames journalism as a public-trust profession; editors and reporters must weigh public welfare above commercial or selfish aims; the canons are intended to codify sound practice and aspirations of American journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: A.N.A. ethical code for advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Code drawn up (1932) covering dishonest or objectionable advertising practices, specifically naming false statements, exaggerations, misleading statements as to price, pseudo-scientific advertising, fake testimonials, offences to decency, and attacks on other industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The code was backed by a Review Committee described as 'a Supreme Court of advertising' to enforce the standards; advertisers and agencies were expected to conform to these prohibitions to maintain ethical advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry self-regulation to control misleading advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation of bodies (A.A.C.W. / National Vigilance Committee / later National Better Business Commission and Better Business Bureaus) to fight dishonest advertising and to police ad content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages advertiser and agency participation in self-regulatory institutions; these organizations set up procedures (paid secretaries, local bureaus) to investigate and curb misleading or objectionable ads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audit Bureau of Circulations standards for reliable circulation statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising promotion demanded more reliable statements of the circulations of individual newspapers; the Audit Bureau of Circulations (A.B.C.) was formed in 1914, with 'careful rules devised for the highly complicated work of the Bureau' cited as key to its success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers and newspapers were expected to submit to standardized auditing procedures so advertisers could rely on circulation figures; although fewer than half of dailies were members in the 1930s, A.B.C. members represented some 90% of aggregate circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: White House press-conference attribution categories and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Hoover established three categories for White House information: (1) that which was specifically designated for direct quotation; (2) background information, which could be used but on which the President could not be quoted; and (3) strictly confidential statements 'off the record.' Roosevelt added a fourth: 'the statement which could be ascribed to him indirectly and without quotes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories constitute norms for using presidential statements and background material: what may be quoted, what may be used anonymously or as background, what is off the record, and what may be paraphrased or attributed indirectly. Practices such as requiring written questions and selective withholding of information are part of this framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal protection against prior censorship and injunctions (Gag Law decision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supreme Court (1931) held the Minnesota 'Gag Law' unconstitutional, noting that 'libel laws afford redress for wrongs committed by publication, but that censorship by injunction is contrary to the Bill of Rights.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes the principle that prior restraints (suppression by injunction) are incompatible with constitutional protections; courts should rely on post-publication remedies such as libel law rather than prior censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection against discriminatory taxation aimed at limiting the press
rubrics_metrics.description: Supreme Court unanimous decision (regarding Louisiana two per cent tax on gross income from advertising) held the tax invalid as 'a deliberate and calculated device in the guise of a tax to limit the circulation of information to which the public is entitled by virtue of the constitutional guarantees.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal standard: taxes or fiscal measures that effectively target the press to inhibit circulation or chill information are unconstitutional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection against piracy of news (AP v. INS)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Associated Press vs. International News Service (1918) the Court held that appropriation of news from early bulletins was unfair competition and there was a remedy in a court of equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations must respect early bulletins and not appropriate competitors' scoops; equitable remedies are available for unfair appropriation of news content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter’s privilege and limits (Elwell case)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a 1921 case a reporter (Hector Elwell) who reported a grand jury indictment before official announcement and refused to reveal his informant was ordered to jail or fined—indicating that at that time federal protection of confidential sources was limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal protection for reporters' confidential sources was not assured at the federal level in this era; some states (e.g., Maryland and later others) enacted statutes to protect reporter–source confidentiality, but journalists should be aware of jurisdictional limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of by-lines to increase story liveliness
rubrics_metrics.description: By-lines on A.P. stories made their advent in 1925; 'The departure had significance, however; it marked a greater liveliness in the stories.' Some editors nonetheless deleted by-lines on the theory that the A.P. logotype was sufficient signature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of by-lines is presented as a practice that can enliven copy and personalize reporting; editors may choose to keep or remove them depending on house style and perceived sufficiency of agency masthead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of propagandic foreign news exchanges
rubrics_metrics.description: A.P. virtually dissolved its agreements for news exchanges with foreign agencies (Reuters, Havas, and Wolffs) when they 'had become too markedly propagandic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations should evaluate the independence and objectivity of their wire partners and avoid formal exchanges that risk importing propaganda; maintaining editorial independence in sourcing is a quality criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government information bureaus: nonpartisan bulletin provision
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Roosevelt departments enlarged their information bureaus and prepared bulletins giving agricultural, statistical, and industrial information 'without political bias.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government press outputs intended for news use should aim for factual, nonpartisan information; journalists can rely on these bureaus for certain factual bulletins but should be alert to potential bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical/legal limits on circulation promotions (no lotteries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulation contests and extensive prize giveaways (e.g., millions in coupons, daily prize money escalating into the tens of thousands) produced huge temporary gains until Postmaster General Hays intervened, calling the scheme a lottery and asking publishers to quit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotional schemes that resemble lotteries or that run afoul of postal/lottery law invite regulatory intervention and may produce only temporary circulation gains; newspapers should design promotions within legal and ethical boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codes of ethics exist but have limited enforcement power
rubrics_metrics.description: The American Society of Newspaper Editors (A.S.N.E.) adopted a code of ethics in 1923 and even attempted to 'put teeth' into it by expelling an editor, but ultimately could not function as a court; 'the Society... was not organized as a court.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional codes (e.g., A.S.N.E. Canons) articulate standards for journalism but enforcement often depends on peer pressure, public opinion, or institutional mechanisms rather than formal judicial powers.
